item.title: Unraveling the K+ transporter gene family in rice: evolution, subcellular localization, K+ uptake activity, and transcriptional responses to salt stress
item.description:
Rice is a global staple food crop, and its yield is seriously limited by soil salinity. The high-affinity K+ transporter/K+ uptake permease/K+ transporter (HAK/KUP/KT) family of potassium transporters plays a pivotal role in K+ homeostasis and plant salt tolerance. However, their systematic characterization and functional relevance to salt tolerance in rice have not been clarified. Here, we conducted genome-wide identification and structural characterization of the HAK/KUP/KT family, assessed their expression profiles under salt stress, and examined their K+ transport function. In total, 27 OsHAK genes were identified in the rice genome, most of which exhibited salt-responsive expression. Yeast functional complementation assays confirmed that OsHAK11, OsHAK13, OsHAK23, OsHAK24, OsHAK25, and OsHAK26 can mediate K+ absorption. Among them, OsHAK11 and OsHAK25 showed relatively strong K+ uptake ability. Subcellular localization analysis revealed that OsHAK11 and OsHAK25 were located in the plasma membrane. Our research systematically analyzed the sequence characteristics of the rice HAK gene family, examined their transcriptional responses to salt stress, and further evaluated the K+ uptake capacity of HAK proteins. These results provide a foundation for further elucidating the function of OsHAKs in plant salt tolerance.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1980352

item.title: Whole-genome duplication reshapes gene–miRNA regulatory networks underlying improved salt stress tolerance in Medicago sativa
item.description:
Abstract

Whole-genome duplication (WGD) is a recurrent feature of plant evolution and crop improvement, yet its direct contribution to abiotic stress tolerance remains difficult to disentangle from hybridization effects. Using full-sibling diploid (2x) and neotetraploid (4x) Medicago sativa genotypes generated through bilateral sexual polyploidization, we investigated how WGD alone reshapes physiological performance and gene–miRNA regulatory networks under salt stress. Neotetraploid plants displayed enhanced tolerance to salinity, maintaining higher chlorophyll content, stomatal conductance, and shoot integrity, alongside reduced visual damage compared with diploid siblings. Transcriptome profiling revealed that ploidy level, rather than salt treatment per se, was the dominant driver of gene expression variation. Indeed, WGD resulted in extensive and largely constitutive transcriptional reprogramming, with more than 2,000 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) distinguishing 4x from 2x plants under both control and saline conditions. By contrast, under salt stress, 705 DEGs specifically differentiated tetraploids from diploids and were enriched in receptor-like kinases, phosphorylation pathways, ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, flavonoid biosynthesis, and WRKY- and MYB-centered regulatory modules. Co-expression network analysis identified salt-associated modules linking signaling and antioxidant pathways with stress-related physiological traits. Small RNA sequencing further showed that WGD reshapes post-transcriptional regulation, with limited salt-induced miRNA changes but the emergence of ploidy-dependent miRNA hubs, including miR2593e and a novel miRNA, targeting signaling and defense-related genes. We hypothesize that WGD establishes a stress-ready regulatory architecture in which coordinated transcriptional and post-transcriptional network rebalancing acts as a buffering system that improves alfalfa physiological performance under salinity, without strong induction of canonical salt-responsive genes.

Journal: Plant Physiology

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1093/plphys/kiag757

item.title: Integrative transcriptomic and functional analyses identify TaARF in the auxin response pathway as a hub gene conferring multi-stage heat tolerance in wheat
item.description:
Heat stress severely impacts the growth, development, and yield of wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) throughout its lifecycle. Identifying key genes regulating heat tolerance is crucial for breeding climate-resilient wheat cultivars. In this study, Zhenongmai 1 (ZNM1), a heat-tolerant wheat cultivar from Zhejiang Province, exhibited a significantly higher seedling survival rate than the heat-sensitive Yangmai 20 after heat stress. At the maturity stage, ZNM1 maintained superior grain yield components under heat stress, retaining 90.05% of its thousand-grain weight (TGW), while YM20 only retained 84.53%. To elucidate the molecular regulatory mechanism underlying heat tolerance in ZNM1, Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA), Gene Ontology (GO), and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses, were performed to screen heat stress-responsive candidate genes. The results revealed that these candidate genes were predominantly enriched in biological processes including auxin metabolism and NAD(P)H dehydrogenase complex assembly, which are critical for wheat heat tolerance regulation. The expression patterns of 11 core candidate genes were verified by quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR), validating the credibility of the transcriptomic data. Heterologous yeast expression assays further confirmed that TaARF positively regulated plant heat tolerance. Additionally, we systematically analyzed the haplotype variations of TaARF among wheat germplasms from different geographical environments and characterized its tissue-specific expression profiles. This study clarifies the key genes and potential molecular pathways associated with wheat heat tolerance, providing valuable gene resources and theoretical references for the genetic improvement of heat-resistant wheat varieties.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1965437

item.title: FAMUS: A Few-Shot Learning Framework for Large-Scale Protein Annotation
item.description:
Abstract

Motivation

Gene function prediction is pivotal in genomic and metagenomic data analysis. Current annotation tools typically rely on the most similar sequence from the query database and struggle to robustly set meaningful hit thresholds, causing a major challenge for reliable annotation.

Results

Here, we present a contrastive learning framework for functional annotation. FAMUS (Functional Annotation Method Using Supervised contrastive learning) compares query sequences to a full array of profile Hidden Markov Models, encoding each sequence’s complete similarity profile, rather than only its top-scoring hit, into a condensed vector space that minimizes the distance between proteins from the same family. Unannotated sequences are incorporated as negative examples during training, enabling robust detection of proteins that fall outside the reference database without requiring user-defined thresholds. FAMUS outperformed KEGG’s native KofamScan for KEGG Orthology annotation and InterPro’s InterProScan for PANTHER family annotation, especially on realistic, sparsely annotated data. We used this approach to build four protein annotation models spanning the KEGG Orthology, InterPro, OrthoDB, and EggNOG databases. FAMUS is a comprehensive, modular framework that supports both pre-defined and user-specific databases. It can be readily integrated into genomic and metagenomic analysis pipelines for accurate, large-scale functional annotation.

Availability and Implementation

All four models are available as a conda package and via our web server at https://app.famus.bursteinlab.org/, and source code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/burstein-lab/famus/ as well as a source code snapshot at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23132542.

Supplementary Information

Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

Journal: Bioinformatics

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btag761

item.title: Genome sequencing and de novo assembly elucidate the genetic basis of grain quality and fragrance in heirloom rice cultivar Mushk Budji
item.description:
Background

Mushk Budji is a premium, GI-tagged, heritage rice landrace of Kashmir valley, J&K, India, distinguished by its short-bold grains, strong aroma, and soft texture. While its morphological and biochemical traits have been documented, no dedicated genomic resource has previously been available. Here we report a de novo genome assembly of Mushk Budji with adequate depth.

Methods

We first-time performed reference guided whole-genome sequencing of Mushk Budji using the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, generating 64.97 Gb of raw data. The genome assembly was achieved using SPAdes and scaffolded using RagTag against the Nipponbare reference. Structural and functional annotations were conducted with AUGUSTUS and curated across NCBI, UniProt, and KEGG databases. The haplotype analysis was performed for loci related to quality using a set of contrasting genotypes.

Results and discussion

The final assembly comprised 378.29 Mb with an N50 of 29.24 Mb and 97.0% BUSCO completeness. A total of 43,434 non-redundant protein-coding genes were identified, with significant enrichment in pathways related to aroma (2-acetyl-1-pyrroline) and starch biosynthesis. Allelic profiling confirmed the characteristic 8-bp deletion in Badh2, conferring fragrance, alongside additional genes shaping quality and adaptability. Unique haplotypes at SSI and RAmy1A, resembling those of temperate japonica variety Koshihikari, were associated with distinct soft and cohesive cooked texture of Mushk Budji . Comparative analyses revealed evolutionary divergence from canonical japonica references at specific loci. Selective signature analyses revealed contrasting evolutionary patterns among major quality genes. SSI showed evidence of balancing selection, whereas GS3 and Badh2 exhibited signatures of strong human-mediated selection, reflecting the historical preference for desirable grain quality and fragrance traits. Genes controlling amylose content and cooking quality (Wx and Alk) were under moderate purifying selection, indicating functional optimization.

Conclusion

The genomics resource generated in the present study establishes Mushk Budji as a distinct temperate japonica landrace with unique allelic combinations underpinning its aroma, texture and adaptability. The dataset provides a foundation for conservation, breeding and functional genomics, ensuring the sustainable utilization of this heritage rice.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1896265

item.title: Chloroplast Genome Evolution, Heteroplasmy, and Inverted Repeat Dynamics in the Elymus Complex (Triticeae, Poaceae): Insights from Single-Molecule Sequencing of Elymus ciliaris and Comparative Analysis of St-Genome Lineages
item.description:
ABSTRACT

Background/Objectives

Elymus sensu lato (Poaceae) is arguably the largest and most complex genus in the tribe Triticeae. It includes hybrids and polyploids based on x=7 chromosomes, all including the St genome, forming a valuable genepool for forage grass and cereal breeding. Analysis of chloroplast genome diversity and structural dynamics is critical for resolving maternal lineages, reticulate evolution and biodiversity across this agronomically important complex, refining their taxonomy, conservation and exploitation.

Methods

We sequenced the complete chloroplast genome (plastome) of Elymus ciliaris (4x=2n=28; StStYY) using ultra-long Oxford Nanopore single-molecule reads and compared it to 77 additional chloroplast genomes representing major St-genome lineages in Elymus s.l. (Pseudoroegneria St; Elymus s.s. StH, StY; Thinopyrum StJ/E; Campeiostachys StYH; Kengyilia StYP). We analyzed structure, nucleotide diversity, inverted repeat (IR) dynamics, and phylogenetic signal.

Results

The E. ciliaris chloroplast genome was 135,008 bp long (38.3% GC) with a canonical quadripartite structure. Single-molecule reads (n=81) revealed heteroplasmy: two Small-Single-Copy (SSC) orientations at 30%:70% frequency, indicating an inversion polymorphism. Across the Elymus group, comparative analysis of chloroplast assemblies showed high structural conservation but lineage-specific IR-boundary shifts. Kengyilia exhibits exceptional IR expansion. Nucleotide diversity hotspots localize to the large single-copy region, especially in StY lineages. Phylogenies recover a monophyletic St-containing clade but do not delineate genera, reflecting reticulate evolution.

Conclusions

Single-molecule sequencing uncovered heteroplasmy with an inversion polymorphism in a single plant of Elymus ciliaris, hidden in short read assemblies. There were no other polymorphisms, as expected for chloroplast sequences. Our analyses showed that a Pseudoroegneria-like St chloroplast genome predominates as the maternal donor across Elymus polyploids. Variable regions and IR dynamics offer strong models for chloroplast genome evolution in reticulate lineages and suggest exploiting plastome variation to complement nuclear biodiversity studies.

Journal: Annals of Botany

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1093/aob/mcag333

item.title: A St‐derived genome contributes to the formation of the wheat BB genome
item.description:
Summary

  • Although substantial efforts have been made to identify the progenitor of the wheat BB genome, the precise donor remains elusive.

  • In this study, we first investigated the origin of the BB genome using a BB‐specific atp6 gene harboring unique 5′‐end sequences, which is present in multiple copies and partially pseudogenized in the BB genome. BLAST searches revealed that multi‐copied atp6 (pseudo)genes occur exclusively in polyploid St‐genome species.

  • An ultrametric phylogeny constructed from genome‐wide single‐copy genes resolved the divergence of Aegilops speltoides (SS genome) and the St genome c . 4 million years ago, coinciding with the estimated origin of the BB genome. Furthermore, genome‐wide single‐nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)‐based allele matching showed that the St genome best explains BB alleles after SS, with an SS : St SNP ratio of 3 : 1, suggesting that the St genome likely contributed to the BB formation via two independent hybridization events with the SS ancestor. Finally, we identified 52 BB‐specific genes to facilitate the search for the true BB donor or the transitional hybrid.

  • This study provides compelling evidence for the St genome's critical contribution to the BB genome and advances our understanding of how the complex hexaploid genome of bread wheat was formed and reshaped over evolutionary time.

Journal: New Phytologist

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1111/nph.71664

item.title: Genome-wide identification of the BES1 gene family and functional study of VcBES1.3 under salt stress in blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum)
item.description:
BES1 (BRI1-EMS-SUPPRESSOR 1) transcription factors mediate brassinosteroid signaling and regulate plant growth, development, and stress responses. The BES1 family has not been characterized in blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum L.). We identified 16 VcBES1 family members and classified them into four groups based on phylogenetic analysis. Promoters of the BES1 genes mainly contain cis -elements associated with abiotic stress and phytohormone signaling. Tissue-specific expression analysis showed that the VcBES1 family is expressed predominantly in roots and stems. All members except VcBES1.8 and VcBES1.9 responded positively to salt stress. Among them, VcBES1.3 displayed the strongest salt induction. The protein accumulated in the nucleus. Overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi) experiments established that VcBES1.3 enhances salt tolerance. This study characterizes the VcBES1 family, defines its tissue-specific and stress-responsive expression patterns, and demonstrate that VcBES1.3 as a positive regulator of salt tolerance in blueberry.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1965422

item.title: Regulation of target gene expression by chromatin-associated protein-coding transcripts in plants
item.description:
Protein-coding transcripts are regarded as intermediates that mediate DNA-to-protein information flow, leaving their noncoding regulatory potential largely underappreciated. Genome-wide profiling of RNA–chromatin interactions in Arabidopsis has uncovered widespread associations between protein-coding transcripts and distinct genomic loci, implying that they possess regulatory functions. Here, we found that BT2 and GSL8 transcripts modulate target gene transcription independently of their protein products through distinct mechanisms. The BT2 transcript represses transcription of its targets CEP2 and MRF4 by forming RNA–DNA triplexes, thereby restricting root growth and promoting flowering, whereas GSL8 acts through a triplex-independent pathway. Our findings unveil intrinsic regulatory activities of protein-coding transcripts, challenging the canonical definition of mRNA function and blurring the functional distinction between coding and noncoding RNAs in the context of genome evolution.

Journal: Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adz4903

item.title: Diffusible signals from Azospirillum brasilense promote rice growth and induce distinct gene expression changes in plant roots
item.description:
Plants form associations with diverse beneficial microbes, including arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi, rhizobia, and plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB). Research on legume-rhizobia symbiosis (LRS) and AM symbiosis has demonstrated that molecular communication between symbiotic partners is essential for initiating these interactions. Genetic and biochemical studies have further identified both plant and microbial signals, as well as host genetic pathways, that regulate these interactions. However, most studies on plant-PGPB interactions have focused on direct application of PGPB to plant roots, leaving the early signaling mechanisms underlying these interactions poorly understood. In this study, we report that diffusible signals from A. brasilense can promote rice growth without direct contact between bacteria and plant roots, 7 days post-treatment (dpt). Using RNA sequencing, we identified 2,516 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in rice roots in response to diffusible signals from A. brasilense at 1 dpt. We identified differential expression of genes involved in flavonoid synthesis, defense responses, receptor activity, transcription factors, and hormone pathways. Comparative transcriptomic analysis of rice roots with or without contact with A. brasilense revealed both shared and unique gene expression patterns. We observed upregulation of certain defense-response genes (PAL, chitinase, thionin), transcription factors (AP2/ERFs, MYBs, WRKYs, and GRAS), and hormone-related (auxin and ethylene) genes without bacterial contact, but downregulation or no differential expression of these genes upon bacterial contact. This pattern suggests that initial induction followed by subsequent suppression of these genes may be crucial for establishing the interaction with A. brasilense. Our transcriptomic analysis also suggests that flavonoids may be required throughout the interaction, whereas nitrate transporters appear to be involved at later stages and likely require contact between plant roots and bacteria. Collectively, our findings reveal that diffusible signals from A. brasilense can promote rice growth and induce distinct gene expression changes in plant roots. These results provide novel insights into the early phase of rice- A. brasilense interaction and highlight the potential for leveraging plant-PGPB signaling mechanisms to enhance crop growth under adverse environmental conditions.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1911178

item.title: LMBD2 interacts with components of the ECH/YIP complex and contributes to post-Golgi trafficking in Arabidopsis
item.description:
Abstract

The plant cell wall, composed primarily of polysaccharides, is essential for normal plant growth and development. Many of these polysaccharides are synthesized within and subsequently secreted via the endomembrane system. Mutations in genes including MURUS3 (MUR3), YPT/RAB GTPase-interacting protein 4 homologs (YIP4a/YIP4b), and ECHIDNA (ECH) result in dwarf plants, which is believed to be a consequence of impaired cell wall polysaccharide secretion. Here, we identify a LMBR1 (Limb Development Membrane Protein 1)-like membrane protein (LMBD2) and find that loss of LMBD2 suppresses the secretion and growth defects in the mur3, yip4a/yip4b, and ech mutants. LMBD2 localizes to the trans-Golgi apparatus and trans-Golgi network (TGN)/early endosome (EE), where it interacts with YIP4b and orchestrates TGN/EE-mediated trafficking. Furthermore, LMBD2 can competitively attenuate the interaction of YIP4b and ECH. Our findings establish LMBD2 as a component of endomembrane trafficking homeostasis in plant cells and offer new insights into endomembrane dynamics and their influence on plant development.

Journal: The Plant Cell

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1093/plcell/koag310

item.title: Pan-genome analysis reveals conservation and diversification of the SWEET gene family in wheat
item.description:
SWEET (Sugars Will Eventually be Exported Transporter) proteins mediate sugar transport and play important roles in plant growth, development, source-sink allocation, and responses to environmental stimuli. However, the conservation and diversification of the SWEET gene family across the wheat pan-genome remain poorly understood. Here, we performed a systematic pan-genome analysis of the SWEET gene family across 19 hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) accessions. A total of 1,594 SWEET genes were identified, with 77–90 members in individual genomes. Gene copies belonging to core, soft-core, dispensable, and private homologous groups accounted for 52.6%, 30.9%, 14.6%, and 1.9%, respectively, based on presence/absence variation (PAV), revealing a predominantly conserved genomic framework accompanied by a smaller accession-variable component. Phylogenetic, motif, chromosomal and synteny analyses further revealed extensive evolutionary and genomic conservation accompanied by localized diversification among family members. Extensive homeologous and inter-accession collinearity was observed, and most pairwise ortholog comparisons exhibited Ka/Ks ratios below 1, supporting predominant purifying selection on conserved SWEET coding sequences. Promoter analysis identified diverse putative cis-regulatory elements related to environmental, hormonal, and developmental regulation, while transcriptome profiling showed heterogeneous tissue- and stress-associated expression patterns among TaSWEET genes. qRT-PCR analysis further suggested distinct temporal responses of selected TaSWEET genes under cold and polyethylene glycol (PEG)-induced osmotic stress. TaSWEET47 overexpression significantly increased grain width, thousand-grain weight, and mature-grain starch content in two independent transgenic lines without significantly affecting grain length. Collectively, these results reveal gene-content, evolutionary, regulatory, and transcriptional diversification within a broadly conserved SWEET family framework.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1949812

item.title: Comparative physiological and photosynthetic responses of three mangrove species to salinity stress and exogenous melatonin
item.description:
Extreme salinity is a major environmental constraint affecting plant growth and physiological performance in coastal ecosystems. Although mangroves are naturally adapted to saline environments, their tolerance and physiological responses vary among species, and the effects of exogenous melatonin (MT) under different salinity levels remain insufficiently understood. This study compared the physiological and photosynthetic responses of Aegiceras corniculatum, Kandelia obovata, and Rhizophora stylosa under NaCl-only and corresponding NaCl + MT treatments. Seedlings were subjected for 84 days to seven treatments: control (T1), 100 mM NaCl (T2), 200 mM NaCl (T3), 400 mM NaCl (T4), 100 mM NaCl + 100 μM MT (T5), 200 mM NaCl + 100 μM MT (T6), and 400 mM NaCl + 100 μM MT (T7). Each species × treatment combination comprised one container–reservoir treatment experimental unit containing five seedling subsamples. At 200 mM NaCl, predicted maximum leaf area (K) was 14.6% and 43.0% higher in A. corniculatum and K. obovata, respectively, under the corresponding NaCl + MT treatment than under NaCl alone. Severe salinity (T4) net photosynthetic rate (PN) was 70.18% and 64.17% lower in A. corniculatum and K. obovata, respectively compared with the control. Whereas R. stylosa maintained comparatively higher photosynthetic activity across treatments. Furthermore, reductions were observed in other photosynthesis parameters, with A. corniculatum showing the greatest sensitivity, whereas R. stylosa maintained higher photosynthetic activity under saline conditions. Maximum PSII quantum efficiency (Fv/Fm) remained within a relatively narrow range across treatments, whereas photochemical and non-photochemical responses differed among species. Pigment responses were also species specific, at 200 mM NaCl, total chlorophyll in K. obovata was 58.0% higher under T6 than under the corresponding NaCl-only treatment (T3). These findings indicate that MT-associated responses varied with mangrove species and salinity level, with the clearest changes in specific growth, gas-exchange, photoprotective, and pigment traits under NaCl treatments. Because no MT-only treatment was included, the independent effect of MT under non-saline conditions could not be evaluated; moreover, the shared container–reservoir design limited independent treatment-level replication.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1966477

item.title: Multidimensional molecular strategies for crop photoperiod adaptation and latitudinal expansion
item.description:
The traditional regional distribution of agriculture was historically constrained by crops’ inherent dependence on local environmental cues, particularly photoperiod and temperature. Natural domestication and artificial selection have progressively reduced this dependence on native ecosystems, resulting in a profound restructuring of global agricultural patterns. From the perspective of this global restructuring, this study systematically examines the multidimensional molecular mechanisms underlying photoperiodic adaptive evolution, including population-level point mutations, epigenetic modifications, structural variations, and copy number variations. In parallel, we propose that the latitudinal adaptive expansion of crops represents not merely an ecological niche shift, but a complex evolutionary process driven by coordinated genetic reprogramming across the genome, epigenome, and transcriptome. Consequently, reshaping future agricultural landscapes requires moving beyond the constraints imposed by individual climatic factors and establishing a multidimensional framework that integrates environment, genetic traits, and ecological adaptation. Moreover, rather than focusing solely on the speed of regional expansion, future molecular design should promote the coordinated improvement of broad-spectrum latitudinal adaptability and elite yield-quality traits, thereby securing global food safety and agricultural sustainability.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1967465

item.title: Genome-wide association mapping reveals stable genomic regions associated with fruit quality traits in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.)
item.description:
Fruit quality has become a primary breeding objective in tomato because it determines consumer acceptance, processing efficiency, and market value. However, quality-related traits are quantitatively inherited and strongly influenced by environmental conditions, making genetic improvement challenging. In this study, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) was conducted to elucidate the genetic architecture of six economically important fruit quality traits, including luminosity, hue, chroma, soluble solids content (°Brix), titratable acidity, and fruit fresh weight (FW), using a diverse panel of 305 tomato accessions evaluated over two growing seasons. Substantial phenotypic variation was observed for all traits, with significant effects of genotype, year, and genotype × year interaction, indicating that fruit quality is governed by both genetic and environmental factors. Fruit weight, luminosity, hue, chroma, and °Brix exhibited high broad-sense heritability, whereas titratable acidity showed moderate heritability. Correlation analysis revealed strong positive relationships among color-related traits, while °Brix was positively associated with acidity but negatively correlated with fruit color attributes and FW. Skim sequencing generated 4,618 high-quality single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and GWAS was performed using multiple models. GWAS identified 15 non-redundant marker-trait associations (MTAs) across chromosomes, with several loci consistently detected across statistical models. A prominent locus, SL4.0ch03_12722521, on chromosome 3 was associated with luminosity, hue, and chroma, explaining up to 53.86% of phenotypic variation (PVE), suggesting pleiotropic regulation of fruit color. Stable loci controlling FW and soluble solids were also identified on chromosome 5, explaining up to 52.88% PVE. Candidate genes of significant MTAs included sucrose synthase, sec14p-like phosphatidylinositol transfer protein, bHLH transcription factor, and chitinase genes, indicating potential roles in carbohydrate metabolism, fruit development, cell wall remodeling, pigmentation, and ripening. These findings provide valuable genomic resources for improving fruit quality and accelerating the development of elite tomato cultivars.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

Original article: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2026.1972937

item.title: cPRIME enables endogenous mapping of genetic variant effects at RNA level
item.description:
Abstract

Understanding the functional consequences of genetic variants, particularly those classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS), is a major challenge in genomics. While variant effects at protein level are well recognized, roles in post-transcriptional regulation are increasingly appreciated. Here, we introduce cPRIME (prime editing with cDNA readout), a scalable method for assessing variant effects at RNA level. cPRIME employs prime editing to insert genetic variants into endogenous genomic loci, followed by the quantification of changes in variant frequencies at RNA (cDNA) and genomic DNA (gDNA) level. We demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse karyotypes and genomic loci and reveal that synonymous marker edits - frequently used in prime editing screens - can themselves alter RNA processing and thereby confound the interpretation of variant effects. Taken together, cPRIME provides a platform for studying the post-transcriptional consequences of genetic variants in their genomic context and establishes a framework for the functional interpretation of RNA-altering variants in cancer and other diseases.

Journal: Nature Communications

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78344-9

item.title: Dynamic Graph Prior-Guided Latent Adaptation for Generalizable Single-Cell Perturbation Response Prediction
item.description:
Abstract

Motivation

Predicting transcriptional responses to drug perturbations in unseen cellular contexts is a central challenge in single-cell perturbation modeling. This challenge creates a need for models that combine flexible state transitions with structured biological prior knowledge. Existing data-driven models often struggle to generalize across unseen cell types, while many prior-based models rely on static biological graphs without explicitly conditioning prior influence on perturbation-specific target support.

Results

We propose DGP-LA, a dynamic graph-prior latent adaptation framework that refines biological priors and injects them as gated latent corrections within a cell-state-conditioned transition model. DGP-LA couples a transition backbone with perturbation-conditioned sparse graph refinement. It propagates gene-aligned target support over the refined graph and selectively injects the resulting topology-aware signal into the hidden representation. On Tahoe and NeurIPS, DGP-LA improves Pearson Delta relative to State by 8.7% and 35.8% for generalization across unseen cell types. In zero-shot drug perturbation response prediction on unseen cell types, it improves Pearson Delta relative to CRISP by 79.1% and 67.6%. The model also improves DE-gene recovery, response discrimination, and Hallmark pathway recovery, supporting adaptive latent integration of biological priors for more generalizable and biologically interpretable perturbation modeling.

Availability

DGP-LA’s source code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/bieyl/DGP-LA and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22155398.

Supplementary information

Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

Journal: Bioinformatics

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btag747

item.title: Pollen tube integrity is critical for thermotolerance in tomato and is enhanced by loss of SlRALF1
item.description:
Reproductive success of angiosperms depends on the ability of pollen to build a highly polarized cellular extension (the pollen tube) that delivers sperm to female gametes for fertilization. This process is highly temperature sensitive, but we lack information about how heat stress affects pollen function and the molecular pathways that impart thermotolerance. Here we show that maintaining cellular integrity during pollen tube germination and extension is the pollen performance parameter that distinguishes thermosensitive from thermotolerant tomato cultivars and that loss-of-function of one of four pollen-expressed Rapid Alkalinization Factor (RALF) signaling peptides can enhance thermotolerance. Moreover, we found that heat stress antagonizes RALF signaling required to maintain patterns of pectin distribution in the pollen tube cell wall to ensure integrity. These findings establish a molecular framework for understanding how pollen tube growth is modulated in response to the environment and show that RALF signaling can be altered to achieve thermotolerant pollen tube growth.

Journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

Original article: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2611706123

item.title: Silicon-mediated alleviation of cadmium stress in Pennisetum glaucum: insights from physiology and root transcriptomics analysis
item.description:
The problem of cadmium (Cd) pollution in soil has attracted much attention. Although Pennisetum glaucum has developed tolerance mechanisms to heavy metals, the accumulation of excess Cd through the food chain threatens human health. Silicon (Si) has a beneficial role in alleviating environmental stress. However, the underlying physiological and molecular mechanisms for alleviating Cd toxicity in P. glaucum are still largely unknown. Therefore, experiments were conducted to explore the effects of Si on the photosynthetic system, antioxidant defense system, and the expression of in P. glaucum under Cd stress. The results showed that Si amendment increased the net photosynthetic rate and chlorophyll content of Cd-stressed P. glaucum by 19.7% and 13.8%, respectively. Moreover, DHAR and MDHAR activities in roots were significantly increased by 53.6% and 63.6% in the AsA-GSH cycle after Si application, while MDA concentration was significantly decreased by 14.6%. Importantly, exogenous Si application dramatically reduced Cd concentration in roots and shoots of P. glaucum by 52.7% and 21.5%, respectively under Cd stress. RNA-seq analysis showed that 6491 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, among which 4429 DEGs were down-regulated and 2062 DEGs were up-regulated. Root transcriptomic analysis revealed that gene expression differed between the Cd and Cd+Si treatments, particularly for genes related to photosynthesis and glutathione metabolism. Contrarily, the expression of genes involved in Cd uptake and transport, such as ABCG36, ABCB11, Nramp5, and Nramp4 (folds were -1.10, -2.52, -2.66, and -1.55, respectively) were down-regulated by the addition of Si. Overall, these above results demonstrate that Si supplementation offers a viable approach to reduce Cd accumulation and ensure the safe production of forage crops.

Journal: Frontiers in Plant Science

item.title: Metabolic and signalling processes in plant cell wall integrity maintenance
item.description:
Abstract

Background

Our understanding of plant cell walls has profoundly changed in recent decades. Originally seen as sturdy recalcitrant structures supporting plant growth, development, and interactions with the environment, we now appreciate the dynamic processes and plasticity modulating cell wall homeostasis, enabling cell walls to perform their respective biological functions in a highly adaptive manner. A key component underlying plasticity and responsible for adaptive changes is the plant cell wall integrity maintenance mechanism. It is responsible for monitoring and maintaining the functional integrity of cell walls by initiating adaptive changes in cell wall composition and structure in response to stimuli arising during growth, development and interactions with the environment.

Scope

Here we provide an overview of our current knowledge of the processes important for plant cell wall structure and homeostasis in the context of cell wall integrity maintenance, summarizing the main components of the cell wall, the cell surface receptors responsible for monitoring the integrity of cell walls, and the mode of action of the cell wall integrity maintenance mechanism for preserving cell wall functions during physiological processes and stress responses.

Conclusions

This overview shows how the cell wall integrity maintenance mechanism ensures the functional integrity of the cell wall and how this is maintained through integration of different stimuli driving tightly controlled, adaptive changes in cell wall homeostasis by involving different receptors and signalling cascades.

item.title: Coordination of lignin and pectin remodeling by a NAC transcription factor regulates seed abscission in sesame ( Sesamum indicum L .)
item.description:
Abstract

Seed shattering, which facilitates seed dispersal, is essential for plant reproduction but causes substantial yield loss in sesame (Sesamum indicum L.). It occurs through capsule dehiscence and/or seed abscission from the placenta, either simultaneously or independently depending on the species. In this study, we investigated cell wall-associated factors underlying delayed seed abscission in the sesame cultivar Suwon195 (SW195) relative to the easy-shattering cultivar IT030100. Histological and transcriptome analyses indicated that cell wall remodeling, particularly involving pectin and lignin, contributes to the delayed abscission phenotype of SW195. SW195 showed higher pectin methylesterase activity and stronger accumulation of low-methyl-esterified homogalacturonan, together with lower polygalacturonase-associated pectin turnover, than IT030100. These changes are consistent with a pectin-remodeling state that favors wall stabilization in the SW195 abscission zone (AZ). AZ lignification was also weaker in SW195. Pharmacological inhibition of lignin biosynthesis altered pectin staining and reduced seed abscission in IT030100, whereas monolignol supplementation restored both phenotypes, supporting a functional association between lignification, pectin-related wall remodeling, and abscission. QTL mapping and whole-genome resequencing identified a major locus on chromosome 9 encompassing a NAC transcription factor (SiNAC; SIN_1025412) and a pectin methylesterase inhibitor (SiPMEI; SIN_1025380). Transient overexpression of SiNAC enhanced lignin biosynthesis in sesame. Together, these findings indicate that coordinated lignin deposition and pectin remodeling are associated with seed abscission in sesame and identify candidate genetic components for breeding reduced-shattering cultivars.

item.title: The energy sensor SnRK1 promotes starvation-induced autophagosome formation by modulating ATG13a phosphorylation in Arabidopsis
item.description:
Abstract

In eukaryotes, autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved cellular degradation and recycling process that is tightly associated with cellular nutrient status. The energy sensor SNF1-RELATED KINASE 1 (SnRK1) is thought to sense nutrient starvation and induce autophagy, but how it regulates autophagosome formation in plant cells remains largely unknown. Here, we show that the SnRK1 α-catalytic subunit KIN10 regulates autophagosome formation in Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) by interacting with and phosphorylating AUTOPHAGY-RELATED PROTEIN 13a (ATG13a), a key component of the ATG1a–ATG13a protein kinase complex involved in autophagy initiation. KIN10 directly phosphorylates ATG13a in vitro and in vivo, inhibiting its ubiquitination and increasing its abundance. Moreover, we identified ten serine residues in ATG13a that are important for KIN10-mediated phosphorylation. Transgenic plants accumulating a nonphosphorylatable ATG13a variant with mutations of these ten residues were less tolerant of starvation than ATG13a-overexpressing plants and displayed accelerated leaf senescence and lower autophagic flux. The KIN10-mediated phosphorylation of ATG13a did not affect ATG1a–ATG13a complex formation; instead, it facilitated ATG1a phosphorylation, thereby promoting autophagosome formation. Therefore, our findings suggest that the KIN10–ATG13a module modulates SnRK1-mediated autophagosome formation, likely representing a key step in integrating energy sensing and autophagy initiation in plant cells.

item.title: Blue light optimizes photosynthetic physiology and photoprotective molecular mechanisms of Hydrangea quercifolia seedlings
item.description:
Introduction

Hydrangea quercifolia is a rare ornamental shrub whose natural populations have declined due to habitat loss, necessitating efficient artificial propagation techniques. Light quality is a critical environmental factor regulating seedling growth and physiological quality; however, the molecular mechanisms by which different LED light spectra modulate photosynthetic physiology and hormone signaling in H. quercifolia remain poorly understood.

Methods

We investigated the regulatory mechanisms of four LED light qualities—white (W), blue (B), red (R), and red:blue = 3:1 (R3B1)—on the growth, photosynthetic performance, chloroplast ultrastructure, hormone metabolism, and transcriptomic profiles of H. quercifolia 'Harmony' seedlings. Physiological parameters were measured on days 7, 14, and 21, and RNA sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes and associated signaling pathways.

Results

Blue (B) light significantly increased chlorophyll, anthocyanin, and cytokinin (CTK) contents, promoted chloroplast proliferation and grana thylakoid development, and enhanced photosynthetic efficiency. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that B light upregulated genes encoding photosystem I (PSI) and photosystem II (PSII) reaction center proteins (especially PsbS, Photosystem II S subunit), strengthened non-photochemical quenching (NPQ) and photoprotective capacity, and reduced brassinosteroid (BR) biosynthesis by suppressing BRI1 (Brassinosteroid Insensitive 1) and BSK (Brassinosteroid-Signaling Kinase) expression. In contrast, R3B1 and red (R) light induced chloroplast shrinkage, reduced chloroplast number, and triggered starch accumulation. R3B1 light inhibited PSII oxygen evolution and electron transport, downregulating chloroplast-related genes; while R light suppressed cytokinin biosynthesis by downregulating CRE1 (Cytokinin Response 1) and activated BAK1 (BRI1-Associated Receptor Kinase 1)-mediated BR signaling.

Discussion

These findings demonstrate that blue light plays a pivotal role in promoting the high-quality development of hydrangea seedlings by optimizing photosynthetic apparatus assembly, enhancing photoprotection, and repressing BR-mediated growth inhibition. The differential molecular responses to distinct light spectra provide a theoretical basis for designing optimized artificial light environments and improving the efficiency of horticultural seedling production.

item.title: Single-Cell and Spatial Perspectives on Source-Sink Dynamics in Plants
item.description:
Abstract

Source-sink relationships describe how plants coordinate carbon production, transport, and utilization to support growth, reproduction, and stress responses. Classical physiological studies established a robust organ-level framework for carbon allocation, but these approaches largely treat tissues as homogeneous units. Recent advances in single-cell and spatial omics technologies now reveal that both sources and sinks consist of diverse cell populations with specialized metabolic and transport functions. In this review, we synthesize emerging insights from single-cell transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics, and integrative multi-omics to show how cellular heterogeneity shapes photosynthetic source strength, vascular transport interfaces, and sink development. We further discuss how stress responses, signaling molecules, and plant-associated microbiomes dynamically reprogram source-sink relationships in a spatially structured manner. Finally, we highlight opportunities to integrate high-resolution molecular atlases with physiological modeling and machine learning approaches to develop predictive frameworks for carbon allocation. These advances suggest that future crop improvement strategies will increasingly rely on cell-type-specific engineering of transport processes and metabolic sinks rather than simply enhancing photosynthesis

item.title: Germplasm evaluation and differentiation in Polygonatum kingianum via chloroplast genome resources
item.description:
Introduction

Polygonatum kingianum (PK) is an important medicinal crop with diverse germplasm that is difficult to distinguish morphologically, particularly at early developmental stages. Misidentification can lead to inappropriate regional cultivation and yield losses when germplasm is introduced into unsuitable environments. Although chloroplast (cp) genomes provide abundant sequence information, variation among PK germplasm groups has not been systematically translated into practical markers for authentication.

Methods

Here, 39 cp genomes representing seven PK germplasm groups and five related Polygonatum species were comparatively analyzed to characterize genomic variation and develop PCR-based markers.

Results

Rather than extensive structural divergence, the genomes exhibited localized sequence variation. In an expanded dataset of 118 PK cp genomes, 1,247 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and 263 indels were identified, with higher variant densities in the single-copy regions than in the inverted repeats. Integration of comparative alignments, nucleotide-diversity profiles, and locus-specific differences identified five regions: ycf2, clpP, rps7-trnV, atpF-atpH, and ycf4-cemA for marker development. Six primer pairs showed 100% amplification and sequencing success in the tested samples and collectively distinguished the tested PK germplasm groups and related Polygonatum species. Phylogenomic analyses further resolved PK as a distinct lineage within sect. Verticillata and revealed cp differentiation among PK germplasm.

Discussion

These findings show that cp genomic variation provides additional molecular resources for PK germplasm authentication and characterization and may support the evaluation and utilization of medicinal crop genetic resources.

item.title: Seumetry: a versatile and comprehensive R toolkit to accelerate high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data analysis
item.description:
Abstract

Motivation

Recent progress in flow and mass cytometry technologies enables the simultaneous measurement of over 50 parameters for an individual cell. The resulting increase in data volume and complexity present challenges for conventional analysis methods, which are based on manual gating, are time-consuming and fail to capture unknown or minor cell populations. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) technologies have prompted the development of computational analysis tools designed to process and analyze high-dimensional biological data. Building on these advances, we here present Seumetry, a framework that combines flow and mass cytometry data-specific analysis methods with the capabilities of Seurat, a powerful tool for the analysis of scRNAseq data.

Results

Seumetry offers methods for advanced quality control, data visualizations, and differential population abundance and protein expression analysis. We tested Seumetry on an in-house generated complex dataset of immune cells from different layers of human intestines, demonstrating that Seumetry accurately identifies distinct immune cell populations. Furthermore, benchmarking against public datasets showed that Seumetry aligns with manual-gated results, further validating its use for high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data. In summary, Seumetry provides a new scalable framework for the comprehensive analysis of high-dimensional cytometry data with seamless integration into commonly used scRNAseq analysis tools, enabling in-depth analysis methods to facilitate biological interpretations.

Availability

Seumetry code is available open source under an MIT license and the current version can be viewed and used via Github: https://github.com/imsb-uke/Seumetry; and archived on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21216681. Flow cytometry data generated for this manuscript is available via Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11935872.

Supplementary information

Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

item.title: Genome-wide analysis of the GATA gene family in Castanea mollissima reveals key regulators involved in salt stress response
item.description:
The GATA gene family comprises important transcription factors (TFs) that affect plant ontogeny and abiotic/biotic stress tolerance. Castanea mollissima is a significant economic and food-producing tree species in the Northern Hemisphere, known for its strong wind resistance and soil stabilization capabilities. Nevertheless, existing studies have not explored the characteristics and functions of the GATA family in C. mollissima . The study identified 21 CmGATA genes from the N11–1 reference genome assembly of C. mollissima, which were dispersed among 12 chromosomes. Phylogenetic analysis helped to categorize these genes into four distinct subfamilies, with genes belonging to the same subfamily exhibiting considerable similarities in terms of structural characteristics and conserved motif composition. Collinear analysis further revealed that the major driver of CmGATA gene family expansion was segmental duplication, followed by evolutionary pressure predominantly shaped by purifying selection. Phenotypic indicators, such as antioxidant enzyme activity, exhibited significant alterations, and transcriptomic analysis revealed increasingly more differentially expressed genes (DEGs) as salt stress treatment continued. Notably, transcriptome analysis demonstrated the expression patterns of CmGATA genes under salt stress, and combined with their correlation with phenotype indicators and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), effectively benefiting the exploration of the function of CmGATA genes in C. mollissima salt stress response. Additionally, validation experiments utilizing reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) demonstrated gene expression trends consistent with those obtained from RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analyses. This study theoretically assists in comprehending the evolution and function of the CmGATA genes under salt stress, offering potential applications in environmental conservation and saline–alkali land improvement. Enhancing salt tolerance in C. mollissima could support its cultivation in a wider range of regions, combining ecological benefits of soil and water conservation with economic value.

item.title: Avirulence genes of Magnaporthe oryzae are a pathogen defense arsenal shaped by cognate rice resistance genes in the field
item.description:
Summary

  • We examined the frequency of and variation in eight avirulence (AVR) genes from 840 Magnaporthe oryzae field isolates collected from the Southern United States relative to rice resistance (R) genes deployed from 1959 to 2017. Little coding or noncoding variation was detected in AVR‐Pi9, AVR‐Pib, ACE1 and AVR‐Pizt, which correspond to R genes not used in the United States.

  • In the United States, AVR‐Pik, corresponding to rice R gene Pi‐k alleles deployed at varying levels since the late 1960s, was present in 37% of the isolates over six decades. AVR‐Pita1, corresponding to Pi‐ta deployed in the late 1990s, reached a low point in the 5‐yr period following Pi‐ta deployment and then recovered to 99% in recent years.

  • Our results suggest a fitness penalty for M. oryzae isolates carrying nonfunctional AVR variants and provide concrete data on how changes in plant R gene composition can impact pathogen populations. These findings will inform localized strategies for R gene usage and durable control of blast disease.

  • AVR frequencies differ over time between United States and global samples for AVR‐Pik, AVR‐Pi9, AVR‐Pii and AVR‐Pita1 . Further whole genome analysis including additional US samples is necessary to confirm whether the United States is a geographically isolated population.

item.title: Distinct phytochrome-specific regulation of tomato sugar metabolism and plant architecture by far-red light
item.description:
Abstract

Phytochromes are a family of plant photoreceptors specialized in detecting red and far-red light (FR). Increased FR levels can trigger the shade avoidance syndrome, typically leading to morphological adjustments enhancing light perception. FR can also increase plant sugar levels by an unknown mechanism, and the roles of individual phytochromes in these responses remain largely unclear. Here, we used reverse genetics and FR trials in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum cv. Moneymaker) to assess the involvement of five phytochromes on different architectural, physiological, and sugar metabolism-related changes. Although FR had no direct positive effect on leaf photosynthesis, overall plant photosynthetic capacity increased, likely due to FR-induced architectural changes improving light capture. We found that phyB2 was involved in regulating this whole-plant photosynthesis response to FR. Our results using phy mutants indicated that FR can also directly affect tomato sugar metabolism independently of architectural and physiological changes. We found a critical role for phyE in regulating carbohydrate levels. We also found that phyB1 and phyB2 regulate source-sink dynamics under FR, and that phyA is potentially a negative regulator of sink strength under FR. Collectively, our work revealed distinct roles for individual phytochromes in coordinating FR-specific architectural and sugar metabolism responses in tomato.

item.title: CRISPR-HAWK: Haplotype- and Variant-Aware Guide Design Toolkit for CRISPR-Cas
item.description:
Abstract

Motivation

Current CRISPR guide RNA design tools rely on reference genomes, overlooking how genetic variation impacts editing outcomes. As genome editing advances toward clinical applications, incorporating population diversity becomes essential for ensuring therapeutic efficacy across diverse populations.

Results

We present CRISPR-HAWK, a framework integrating individual- and population-scale variants and haplotypes into gRNA design. Analyzing therapeutic targets across 79,648 genomes reveals that genetic variants substantially alter guide performance. For the clinically approved sickle cell disease therapeutic guide targeting BCL11A, we identify haplotypes that completely abolish predicted cutting activity. Across seven therapeutic loci, 82.5% of guides contain variants modifying on-target activity. Variants also create novel protospacer adjacent motif sites generating individual-specific guides invisible to reference-based design. These findings demonstrate that variant-aware selection is critical for equitable genome editing.

Availability

CRISPR-HAWK is available at https://github.com/pinellolab/CRISPR-HAWK and https://github.com/InfOmics/CRISPR-HAWK.

Supplementary information

Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
